topics.name: Parkinson’s disease
topics.kicker: Brain disease that affects movement · Linked to loss of dopamine-making cells
topics.briefing: Parkinson’s disease is a brain disorder that slowly makes movement harder, often starting with a shaking hand, stiff muscles, or slow steps. It happens as nerve cells in a small, dark region of the brain, the substantia nigra, are slowly lost, leaving too little dopamine, a chemical messenger that helps control movement. English surgeon James Parkinson described it in 1817, and a medicine called levodopa, which the brain turns into dopamine, helps many people with the disease.
topics.answerHtml: Parkinson’s disease (accept Parkinson disease or paralysis agitans; prompt on parkinsonism or shaking palsy; do not accept “Alzheimer’s disease” or “Huntington’s disease”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1912, Friedrich Lewy described round clumps of protein inside the nerve cells of people with this disease, and those clumps are now called Lewy bodies. They are made largely of a protein called alpha-synuclein [“sih-NOO-klee-in”].
tossups.r: In this disease, dopamine-making cells in the brain are lost. For 10 points, name this movement disorder that often causes a tremor in a resting hand.

tossups.p: Arvid Carlsson shared the 2000 Nobel Prize in medicine partly for showing that animals given the drug reserpine became slow and stiff, much like people with this disease, until they received L-DOPA. His work showed that dopamine is a brain messenger in its own right.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease in which dopamine-making brain cells are slowly lost, causing tremors and slow movement.

tossups.p: In the book _Awakenings_, Oliver Sacks described how the drug L-DOPA in 1969 briefly brought back movement to patients who had barely been able to move for decades because of a condition with this disease’s symptoms. Robin Williams starred in a 1990 film of that story.
tossups.r: Doctors give L-DOPA for this disease because the brain turns it into dopamine. For 10 points, name this movement disorder.

tossups.p: In 1960, Oleh Hornykiewicz [“hor-nee-KEH-vitch”] found that the brains of people who had this disease contained far less dopamine than normal. Later that decade, George Cotzias [“KOT-see-us”] showed that large doses of levodopa taken by mouth could ease this disease’s symptoms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this brain disease that causes tremors, stiff muscles, and slow movement.

tossups.p: People with this disease may develop micrographia [“my-kroh-GRAF-ee-uh”], handwriting that becomes smaller and more cramped, and their faces may show less expression. Losing the sense of smell can be one of this disease’s earliest signs, years before any movement problems.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease that causes a shaking tremor and slow movement, named for an English surgeon.

tossups.p: In deep brain stimulation, surgeons place thin wires in a region such as the subthalamic [“sub-thuh-LAM-ik”] nucleus to send gentle electrical pulses that calm this disease’s tremors. Many people with this disease take levodopa together with carbidopa, which stops the body from turning levodopa into dopamine before it reaches the brain.
tossups.r: This disease is linked to the loss of dopamine-making cells in the substantia nigra. For 10 points, name this disease that causes tremors and slow movement.

tossups.p: A world awareness day for this disease is held on April 11, the birthday of the English surgeon who described it in _An Essay on the Shaking Palsy_ in 1817. Decades later, the French doctor Jean-Martin Charcot [“shar-KOH”] suggested renaming the disease after that surgeon.
tossups.r: Muhammad Ali was diagnosed with it in 1984. For 10 points, name this disease of tremors and slow movement.

tossups.p: The pigment neuromelanin [“noor-oh-MEL-uh-nin”] darkens the brain region hit hardest by this disease, a region whose Latin name means “black substance.” That region of the midbrain normally sends dopamine to the basal ganglia, which help control movement.
tossups.r: That region is the substantia nigra [“sub-STAN-shuh NYE-gruh”]. For 10 points, name this disease that causes tremors and stiffness.

tossups.p: The actor who starred in the _Back to the Future_ movies revealed in 1998 that he had this disease, and in 2000 he started a foundation to fund research on it. Boxer Muhammad Ali, who was diagnosed with this disease in 1984, lit the Olympic flame at the 1996 Atlanta Games.
tossups.r: It is linked to the loss of dopamine-making brain cells. For 10 points, name this disease that causes tremors, stiffness, and slow movement.

tossups.p: Doctors call the classic shaking of this disease a “pill-rolling” tremor, because the thumb and fingers rub together as if rolling a small pill between them. That tremor is usually strongest when the hand is resting and fades when the person reaches for something.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease linked to the loss of dopamine-making neurons in the brain.

tossups.p: Medical students remember this disease’s four main signs with the word TRAP: tremor, rigidity, akinesia [“ay-kih-NEE-zhuh”] or slowness, and postural instability, which means trouble with balance. Many people with this disease walk with short, shuffling steps.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this movement disorder linked to a loss of the brain chemical dopamine.

tossups.p: Doctors cannot treat this disease with dopamine itself, because dopamine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier. Instead they use levodopa, which crosses into the brain and is then converted into dopamine.
tossups.r: This disease damages dopamine-making cells in the substantia nigra. For 10 points, name this disease that often begins with a tremor in one hand.

tossups.p: This disease is the second most common neurodegenerative disease after Alzheimer’s, and it usually begins after age 60. Unlike Huntington’s disease, which is caused by a change in a single inherited gene, this disease usually has no single known cause.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease that slowly makes movement harder, often starting with a tremor in one hand.

tossups.p: In this disease, a shortage of dopamine reaching the striatum [“stry-AY-tum”], a part of the basal ganglia, makes it hard for the brain to start and smoothly control movements. Some people with this disease suddenly “freeze” in place when trying to walk through a doorway.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disorder whose symptoms include a resting tremor and stiff muscles.

tossups.p: Pope John Paul II and Janet Reno, the U.S. attorney general from 1993 to 2001, both had this disease. Some people with this disease develop a softer, quieter voice, along with stiff muscles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this brain disease that causes tremors and slow movement and is often treated with levodopa.

trap.title: Which brain disease?
trap.body: Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s, and Huntington’s diseases all slowly damage the brain, so their clues get mixed up. Alzheimer’s mainly affects memory and is marked by plaques and tangles; Huntington’s is caused by a single inherited gene and brings sudden, jerky movements. Don’t be fooled by Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome either: it is a heart rhythm condition with no link to this disease.
trap.fix: Dopamine, the substantia nigra, Lewy bodies, levodopa, a resting “pill-rolling” tremor, or Michael J. Fox mean Parkinson’s disease. Memory loss with plaques and tangles means Alzheimer’s; one inherited gene with jerky movements means Huntington’s.
trap.line: Real answer line: Parkinson’s disease (accept Parkinson disease; prompt on parkinsonism; do not accept “Alzheimer’s disease”)

topics.name: Leprosy
topics.kicker: Bacterial disease of the skin and nerves · Curable with multidrug therapy
topics.briefing: Leprosy, also called Hansen’s disease, is an infection caused by a slow-growing bacterium related to the one that causes tuberculosis. It mainly affects the skin and the nerves of the hands, feet, and face, and it can take years to show symptoms. For centuries, people with leprosy were feared and forced to live apart, but since the 1980s a combination of antibiotics called multidrug therapy has cured millions of people.
topics.answerHtml: Leprosy (accept Hansen’s disease; prompt on Mycobacterium leprae; do not accept “tuberculosis”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The bacterium that causes this disease still cannot be grown on lab dishes, so scientists grow it in mouse footpads and in nine-banded armadillos, whose cool bodies suit it. In people, that bacterium prefers cooler parts of the body, such as the skin and the nerves just beneath it.
tossups.r: Gerhard Armauer Hansen identified that bacterium in 1873. For 10 points, name this disease that can damage the skin and nerves.

tossups.p: In 1941, Guy Faget began treating patients with this disease using a drug called Promin at a national hospital in Carville, Louisiana, a success called the “Miracle at Carville.” A related, cheaper pill, dapsone, later became a standard treatment for this disease.
tossups.r: It is now cured with a mix of antibiotics called multidrug therapy. For 10 points, name this bacterial disease of the skin and nerves.

tossups.p: A Belgian priest named Damien [“DAY-mee-un”] cared for people with this disease at Kalaupapa [“kah-lah-oo-PAH-pah”] on the Hawaiian island of Molokai and caught it himself; he was declared a saint in 2009. Mother Marianne Cope, who also served people with this disease on Molokai, was declared a saint in 2012.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease caused by a bacterium related to the one that causes tuberculosis.

tossups.p: Surgeon Paul Brand showed that much of the damage linked to this disease comes from injuries that people do not notice, because the disease harms the nerves that sense pain. Despite a common myth, this disease does not make fingers and toes simply fall off.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this bacterial disease, curable with multidrug therapy, that can numb the hands and feet.

tossups.p: Baldwin IV became King of Jerusalem in 1174 at age 13 even though he had this disease, and three years later he defeated Saladin at the Battle of Montgisard [“mohn-zhee-ZAR”]. In medieval Europe, many people with this disease were made to live apart in special houses outside towns.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease of the skin and nerves, which is now curable with antibiotics.

tossups.p: In Lew Wallace’s 1880 novel _Ben-Hur_, the hero’s mother and sister catch this disease while in prison and are later healed. The Gospels describe Jesus healing people with this disease, which was greatly feared in the ancient world.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this bacterial disease that affects the skin and nerves and is now curable with multidrug therapy.

tossups.p: Raoul Follereau [“foh-luh-ROH”] of France started a world awareness day for this disease in 1954, held on the last Sunday of January, near the anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi’s death. Gandhi was known for caring for people with this disease.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this bacterial disease, curable with multidrug therapy, that can damage nerves in the hands and feet.

tossups.p: Doctors divide this disease into a milder “tuberculoid” form, with only a few light-colored, numb skin patches, and a more severe form with many patches and huge numbers of bacteria. Its bacterium multiplies very slowly, so symptoms can take years to appear.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease caused by a bacterium related to the tuberculosis germ.

tossups.p: Like the tuberculosis germ, the bacterium behind this disease has a waxy cell wall that holds on to red dye in an “acid-fast” stain. That bacterium divides only about once every two weeks, far more slowly than most bacteria.
tossups.r: In 1873, Norwegian doctor Gerhard Armauer Hansen identified it, one of the first germs linked to a human disease. For 10 points, name this disease of the skin and nerves.

tossups.p: In the southern United States, nine-banded armadillos carry the bacterium that causes this disease and have passed it to some people. Most people who are exposed to that bacterium never get sick, because their immune systems fight it off.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease, now curable with a mix of antibiotics, that affects the skin and nerves.

tossups.p: The World Health Organization’s multidrug therapy for this disease combines dapsone, rifampicin [“rih-FAM-pih-sin”], and clofazimine [“kloh-FAZ-ih-meen”], and it has been given free of charge around the world since 1995. That treatment has cured millions of people.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease caused by a slow-growing bacterium related to the one that causes tuberculosis.

tossups.p: India reports more new cases of this disease each year than any other country, followed by Brazil and Indonesia. In 2000, the World Health Organization announced that this disease had been eliminated “as a public health problem” worldwide, meaning fewer than one case for every 10,000 people.
tossups.r: Its germ is a cousin of the tuberculosis germ. For 10 points, name this disease that can numb the hands and feet.

tossups.p: Many patients and doctors prefer another name for this disease, one that honors the Norwegian doctor who found its cause, because its usual name carries centuries of fear and unfair treatment. In the 1900s, many Americans with this disease were sent to live at a hospital in Carville, Louisiana.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease of the skin and nerves, caused by a bacterium related to tuberculosis.

tossups.p: Starting in 1866, the Kingdom of Hawaii sent people with this disease to live in isolation on the Kalaupapa peninsula of Molokai, a place cut off by towering sea cliffs. That settlement became a national historical park in 1980.
tossups.r: A Belgian priest, Father Damien, served the people there. For 10 points, name this bacterial disease of the skin and nerves.

tossups.p: Medieval hospitals for people with this disease were often called lazar houses, after Lazarus, a poor, sick man in one of Jesus’s parables. In the Hebrew Bible, the word tzaraath [“tsah-RAH-aht”], often translated as the name of this disease, covers several different skin conditions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease, caused by a bacterium related to tuberculosis, that can damage nerves.

trap.title: Not tuberculosis!
trap.body: The germ that causes this disease is a close cousin of the tuberculosis germ: both are slow-growing, acid-fast bacteria, and their discoveries came only nine years apart (Hansen in 1873, Robert Koch in 1882). Answer lines want the disease, so naming the germ may only earn a prompt. Also remember that in the Bible, the word translated as “leprosy” covered several skin conditions.
trap.fix: Numb skin patches, hands and feet that lose feeling, armadillos, Molokai, Father Damien, Hansen, or Carville mean leprosy. Coughing, the lungs, or Robert Koch mean tuberculosis. If you say the germ’s name, be ready to name the disease.
trap.line: Real answer line: Leprosy (accept Hansen’s disease; prompt on Mycobacterium leprae; do not accept “tuberculosis”)

topics.name: Species
topics.kicker: Basic unit of classification · Members can interbreed and have fertile young
topics.dates: Two-part names became standard with Linnaeus in 1753
topics.briefing: A species is a group of living things so alike that they can mate and have young that can someday have young of their own. Lions are one species and tigers another, and while a horse and a donkey can produce a mule, mules are almost always sterile. Since Carl Linnaeus in the 1700s, every species gets a two-part Latin name, like Homo sapiens for humans: first the genus, then a second word for the species.
topics.answerHtml: Species (accept biological species; prompt on taxon; do not accept “genus” or “speciation”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Ernst Mayr’s 1942 definition of this term describes groups of populations that actually or potentially interbreed and are reproductively isolated from other such groups. That “biological” concept of this term does not work well for organisms that reproduce without mating, such as bacteria.
tossups.r: Members of one of these groups can mate and produce fertile offspring. For 10 points, name this basic rank of classification, which comes just below genus.

tossups.p: Ensatina [“en-suh-TEE-nuh”] salamanders form a “ring” of populations around California’s Central Valley in which neighbors can interbreed, but the two ends of the ring, which meet in southern California, rarely do. That pattern makes it hard to decide where one of these groups ends and the next begins.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this taxonomic rank, just below genus, whose members can mate and have fertile young.

tossups.p: Hybrid sterility is a postzygotic [“post-zye-GOT-ik”] barrier that keeps two of these groups separate even when they mate and produce offspring. Because the mules born to horses and donkeys are almost always sterile, horses and donkeys count as two different examples of this rank.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this basic unit of biological classification, whose members can breed and have fertile young.

tossups.p: Prezygotic [“pree-zye-GOT-ik”] barriers, such as different mating seasons or different courtship displays, can stop two of these groups from interbreeding before an egg is ever fertilized. Eastern and Western meadowlarks look almost alike but are separate examples of this rank, partly because they sing different songs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rank of classification, below genus, given by the two words of a scientific name like Homo sapiens.

tossups.p: A single preserved specimen called a holotype [“HOL-oh-type”] serves as the official reference for the scientific name of one of these groups. A scientist who discovers a new one of these groups must publish a formal description of it along with a Latin-style name.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this basic unit of classification, whose members can interbreed, named with a genus plus a second word.

tossups.p: In a 1753 book on plants, Carl Linnaeus made it standard to name each of these groups with two Latin words: a capitalized genus followed by a lowercase “specific epithet.” That naming system, whose names are printed in italics, is called binomial nomenclature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this most specific basic rank of classification, such as Homo sapiens for humans.

tossups.p: A 2011 study estimated that Earth holds about 8.7 million of these groups of organisms whose cells have a nucleus, most of which have never been described. Beetles have more named examples of this rank than any other order of animals.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this basic unit of classification, whose members can mate and have fertile offspring.

tossups.p: Harris’s antelope squirrel lives south of the Grand Canyon, while the closely related white-tailed antelope squirrel lives north of it, a classic case of a barrier splitting a population into two of these groups. That kind of split, caused by geographic separation, is called “allopatric” [“al-oh-PAT-rik”].
tossups.r: New ones form through a process called speciation. For 10 points, name this basic unit of classification just below genus.

tossups.p: A 1973 law signed by Richard Nixon protects threatened and endangered examples of this rank in the United States, and the bald eagle was taken off that law’s list in 2007 after its numbers recovered. The California condor is among the groups protected by that law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this basic unit of classification, whose members can interbreed and produce fertile offspring.

tossups.p: Ecologist Robert Paine removed Pisaster [“pih-ZAS-ter”] sea stars from tide pools and found that mussels took over, showing that some of these groups have an outsized effect on their ecosystems. Paine called such a group a “keystone,” after the center stone that holds up an arch.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this basic unit of classification, named by the two words of a scientific name like Tyrannosaurus rex.

tossups.p: Under the phylogenetic [“fye-loh-juh-NET-ik”] concept of this term, one of these groups is the smallest set of organisms that share a common ancestor and can be told apart from all others. Because biologists use many competing definitions of this term, their debate is called this term’s “problem.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this basic rank of classification, whose members can usually mate and have fertile young.

tossups.p: Martha, the last known passenger pigeon, died at the Cincinnati Zoo in 1914, and with her, that group at this level of classification was gone forever. The dodo of the island of Mauritius is another example of this rank that has gone extinct.
tossups.r: In the memory aid “King Philip Came Over For Good Soup,” this rank is the “Soup.” For 10 points, name this most specific basic rank in taxonomy.

tossups.p: In an 1855 paper written in Sarawak on the island of Borneo, Alfred Russel Wallace argued that each new one of these groups appears near a closely related one that already exists.
tossups.r: Four years later, Charles Darwin published a book explaining how these groups originate. For 10 points, name this basic unit of classification whose members can interbreed.

tossups.p: The tenth edition of Carl Linnaeus’s _Systema Naturae_, published in 1758, is the official starting point for scientific names of animals at this rank, including Homo sapiens, which means “wise man.”
tossups.r: This rank sits just below genus. For 10 points, name this rank whose members can interbreed and have fertile young.

tossups.p: Lions and tigers can produce hybrid cubs called ligers in zoos, but the two cats do not interbreed in the wild, so they remain separate examples of this rank. Polar bears and grizzly bears, though, have occasionally had hybrid cubs in the wild.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this basic unit of classification, whose members can interbreed and have fertile young.

trap.title: Species, genus, or speciation?
trap.body: In a two-part name like Homo sapiens, the first word is the genus, the rank just above, and the species is named by both words together. Speciation, the process that forms new species, is a separate answer line, and so is genus. Breeds don’t count either: every dog breed belongs to the same species.
trap.fix: “Members can interbreed,” “fertile offspring,” or “the rank just below genus” means species. “The rank above,” or the capitalized first word of a scientific name, means genus. If the question asks for “this process” that splits one group into two, say speciation.
trap.line: Real answer line: Species (do not accept “genus” or “speciation”)

topics.name: Gallbladder
topics.kicker: Small pouch under the liver · Stores bile and squeezes it out to digest fat
topics.dates: Holds only a few tablespoons of bile
topics.briefing: The gallbladder, a small, pear-shaped pouch tucked under the liver, stores and concentrates bile, a greenish fluid the liver makes all day long. When a fatty meal arrives, a hormone called CCK makes it squeeze bile into the small intestine, where bile breaks fat into tiny droplets. Sometimes bile hardens into gallstones, and doctors can remove the whole organ, because people can live without it.
topics.answerHtml: Gallbladder (accept gall bladder; prompt on biliary system; do not accept “liver,” “pancreas,” or “bile duct”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1882, the German surgeon Carl Langenbuch [“LAHNG-en-bookh”] performed the first successful operation to remove this organ, which is now one of the most common surgeries. People can live without this organ, because the liver can still send its fluid straight to the intestine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this small, pear-shaped organ that stores bile made by the liver.

tossups.p: The hormone cholecystokinin [“koh-luh-sis-toh-KY-nin”], whose name means “bile sac mover,” is released by the duodenum when fatty food arrives and makes this organ contract. At the same time, the sphincter of Oddi [“ODD-ee”] relaxes so this organ’s contents can flow into the intestine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ that stores bile and releases it to help digest fats.

tossups.p: Horses, deer, and rats all lack this organ, so bile flows straight from their livers into their intestines. In humans, this organ makes the bile it holds more concentrated by absorbing water from it between meals.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this small, pear-shaped organ tucked under the liver, where gallstones can form.

tossups.p: A medicine that can slowly dissolve some of the stones that form in this organ is named for bears, because its main chemical was first found in bear bile. Most of those stones are made largely of cholesterol, while others are dark “pigment” stones.
tossups.r: Those stones are called gallstones. For 10 points, name this organ that stores bile from the liver.

tossups.p: King Goujian [“GOH-jyen”] of Yue is said to have tasted the bitter fluid stored in this organ every day to remind himself of a defeat, a story behind a Chinese saying about perseverance. In Chinese, having a “big” one of these organs means being bold or brave.
tossups.r: The liver makes that fluid, called bile. For 10 points, name this organ beneath the liver that stores bile.

tossups.p: This organ is divided into a rounded fundus, a body, and a narrow neck, which leads into the cystic duct. The cystic duct joins the common hepatic duct from the liver to form the common bile duct.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this small organ that stores and concentrates bile, where gallstones can form.

tossups.p: Doctors check for Murphy’s sign, named for the surgeon John B. Murphy, by pressing below the right ribs as a patient breathes in, to see whether this organ is inflamed. Inflammation of this organ, often caused by a stone blocking its duct, is called cholecystitis [“koh-luh-sis-TY-tis”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pear-shaped organ, which can be removed if gallstones form in it.

tossups.p: Ultrasound scans are usually the first test doctors use to look for stones in this organ, which show up as bright spots that cast dark “shadows” on the screen. Those stones can form when bile holds more cholesterol than it can dissolve.
tossups.r: Removing this organ is one of the most common surgeries. For 10 points, name this organ that stores bile, where gallstones form.

tossups.p: This organ releases a fluid whose salts emulsify fats, breaking large fat globules into tiny droplets that the enzyme lipase can digest more easily. That fluid, which this organ stores but does not make, contains no digestive enzymes of its own.
tossups.r: The liver makes that fluid. For 10 points, name this organ that stores bile until a fatty meal arrives.

tossups.p: A stone that slips out of this organ and blocks the common bile duct can cause jaundice, a yellowing of the skin and eyes from a buildup of bilirubin [“bil-ih-ROO-bin”]. This organ sits in the upper right part of the abdomen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this small, pear-shaped organ that stores bile from the liver.

tossups.p: Starting in the late 1980s, surgeons began removing this organ through a few tiny cuts, using a camera on a thin tube, in a “laparoscopic” [“lap-uh-roh-SKOP-ik”] operation that soon became the usual method. The medical name for that operation is cholecystectomy [“koh-luh-sis-TEK-tuh-mee”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ that stores bile and can be removed if stones form in it.

tossups.p: The greenish-yellow color of the fluid stored in this organ comes from pigments such as bilirubin, which forms when old red blood cells are broken down. That fluid is made by the liver and reaches this organ through the cystic duct.
tossups.r: Hardened lumps called gallstones can form inside it. For 10 points, name this pouch under the liver that stores and concentrates bile.

tossups.p: Most stones in this organ never cause symptoms, but a stone that blocks its outlet can cause a sudden pain under the right ribs, called biliary colic, often after a fatty meal.
tossups.r: Those stones are called gallstones. For 10 points, name this organ that stores bile and squeezes it into the small intestine.

tossups.p: Fluid from this organ and juice from the pancreas enter the duodenum together through an opening called the ampulla of Vater [“FAH-ter”]. A stone from this organ that gets stuck there can inflame the pancreas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ, which stores bile between meals and sits under the liver.

tossups.p: Between meals, this organ makes the fluid it stores several times stronger by pulling water out of it, so it needs to hold only a few tablespoons. A fatty meal makes this organ’s muscular walls squeeze.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ that receives bile from the liver through the cystic duct.

The name cholecystokinin means “bile sac mover”
When it contracts, the sphincter of Oddi relaxes to let bile flow into the duodenum

Divided into a rounded fundus, a body, and a narrow neck

trap.title: Liver or gallbladder?
trap.body: The liver makes bile, but the gallbladder only stores and concentrates it, so a clue like “produces bile” wants the liver. The pancreas is a third neighbor whose duct meets the bile duct, and all three send juices into the duodenum. Gallstones themselves, or the bile duct a stone can block, are separate answers too.
trap.fix: “Makes” or “produces” bile means the liver. “Stores,” “concentrates,” or “squeezes out” bile, CCK making it contract, gallstones forming inside it, or a cholecystectomy means the gallbladder. Insulin or digestive enzymes mean the pancreas.
trap.line: Real answer line: Gallbladder (accept gall bladder; do not accept “liver” or “bile duct”)

topics.name: Nematodes
topics.kicker: Unsegmented roundworms · Includes the famous lab worm C. elegans
topics.dates: First animal genome sequenced: C. elegans, 1998
topics.briefing: Nematodes, or roundworms, are smooth, unsegmented worms named for the Greek word for “thread,” and they may be the most numerous animals on Earth, living in soil, in oceans, and inside plants and animals. Some, like hookworms and pinworms, are parasites, but the see-through soil worm _Caenorhabditis elegans_ is a lab superstar: it was the first animal to have its whole genome read, and studying it has led to several Nobel Prizes.
topics.answerHtml: Nematodes (accept roundworms or Nematoda; prompt on worms; do not accept “flatworms” or “annelids”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Victor Ambros and Gary Ruvkun shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering microRNAs, tiny gene-controlling RNA molecules, in a species of these animals. The first microRNA they found, lin-4, controls the timing of that species’ growth through its larval stages.
tossups.r: These animals have a tough outer cuticle that they shed as they grow. For 10 points, name this phylum of unsegmented worms that includes hookworms.

tossups.p: Andrew Fire and Craig Mello won a 2006 Nobel Prize after they injected double-stranded RNA into one of these animals and found that it silenced the matching gene, a process called RNA interference. Their test subject was a see-through species about one millimeter long that eats bacteria in soil.
tossups.r: Members of this phylum have a body cavity called a pseudocoelom [“SOO-doh-SEE-lum”]. For 10 points, name this phylum of worms that includes the lab species _Caenorhabditis elegans_ [“SEE-noh-rab-DY-tiss EL-uh-ganz”].

tossups.p: John Sulston watched every cell division in a living species of these animals to map its complete cell lineage, showing that exactly 131 cells die by programmed cell death as a hermaphrodite develops. Sydney Brenner, who had chosen that species as a model organism, shared a 2002 Nobel Prize with Sulston and H. Robert Horvitz.
tossups.r: That species’ adult hermaphrodites have exactly 959 body cells. For 10 points, name this phylum of unsegmented worms that also includes hookworms and pinworms.

tossups.p: Canisters holding these animals survived the 2003 disaster in which the space shuttle _Columbia_ broke apart over Texas, and they were found alive in the wreckage. The species on that flight grows from an egg into an adult in about three days, one reason it is popular in labs.
tossups.r: That species, _Caenorhabditis elegans_, is a tiny soil worm. For 10 points, name this phylum of cylindrical, unsegmented worms.

tossups.p: In 2011, scientists described the “devil worm,” _Halicephalobus mephisto_, a member of this phylum found living more than a kilometer underground in a South African gold mine. Nathan Cobb, who studied these animals for the U.S. Department of Agriculture, wrote that a film of them would still outline Earth’s landscape if everything else vanished.
tossups.r: These animals’ name comes from the Greek word for “thread.” For 10 points, name this phylum of unsegmented worms that includes hookworms and pinworms.

tossups.p: William Campbell and Satoshi Ōmura [“OH-moo-rah”] shared a 2015 Nobel Prize for discovering avermectin, which led to the drug ivermectin. That drug is given out free in many countries to fight river blindness, a disease caused by one of these worms and spread by the bites of black flies.
tossups.r: Other members of this phylum, spread by mosquitoes, cause elephantiasis. For 10 points, name this phylum of worms that includes hookworms and heartworms.

tossups.p: The Carter Center, founded by former president Jimmy Carter, has led a campaign that cut cases of a disease caused by one of these worms from about 3.5 million in 1986 to fewer than 30 a year in the 2020s. People catch that disease, Guinea worm disease, by drinking water containing tiny water fleas that carry its larvae.
tossups.r: Hookworms and pinworms also belong to this phylum. For 10 points, name this phylum of unsegmented worms with a tough outer cuticle.

tossups.p: John D. Rockefeller funded a 1909 commission to fight a disease caused by one kind of these worms across the American South, where many children went barefoot. That kind’s genus name, _Necator_, means “killer,” and its young larvae enter the body through the skin of bare feet.
tossups.r: That kind is commonly called the hookworm. For 10 points, name this phylum of worms that also includes the lab species _C. elegans_.

tossups.p: Eating undercooked pork or wild game can cause trichinosis [“trik-ih-NOH-sis”], a disease caused by members of this phylum whose larvae curl up inside tiny cysts in muscle. Those parasites belong to the genus _Trichinella_ [“trik-ih-NEL-uh”], whose name refers to their hair-like thinness.
tossups.r: Another member of this phylum, _Ascaris_ [“AS-kuh-riss”], can grow longer than a foot. For 10 points, name this phylum of unsegmented worms that also includes hookworms.

tossups.p: Along with arthropods, these animals are placed in a group called Ecdysozoa [“ek-dih-soh-ZOH-uh”] because they molt their outer covering as they grow. Biologists call them pseudocoelomates [“soo-doh-SEE-loh-mayts”], since their fluid-filled body cavity is only partly lined by tissue from the embryo’s middle layer, the mesoderm.
tossups.r: Their muscles run only lengthwise, so they move by whipping their bodies back and forth. For 10 points, name this phylum of unsegmented worms that includes hookworms.

tossups.p: Cynthia Kenyon found that a single change in a gene called daf-2 roughly doubled the lifespan of a species of these animals. When food runs short, young members of that species can enter a tough, resting “dauer” [“DOW-er”] stage, named for a German word meaning “lasting.”
tossups.r: Hermaphrodites of that species, _C. elegans_, have exactly 302 nerve cells. For 10 points, name this phylum of worms that includes hookworms and pinworms.

tossups.p: In 1986, a team including John White and Sydney Brenner published the first complete wiring diagram of an animal’s nervous system, mapping the connections among the nerve cells of a species of these animals. In 1998, that species became the first animal to have its complete genome sequenced.
tossups.r: That species is a see-through soil worm about one millimeter long. For 10 points, name this phylum of unsegmented worms that also includes hookworms.

tossups.p: Root-knot species of these animals cause swellings called galls on plant roots, and the soybean cyst species is one of the worst pests of soybean crops in the United States. Farmers sometimes plant marigolds, whose roots release chemicals that are toxic to these tiny soil animals.
tossups.r: Others are parasites of people, such as hookworms and pinworms. For 10 points, name this phylum of unsegmented worms.

tossups.p: Martin Chalfie shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry after he made a jellyfish’s green fluorescent protein glow inside the nerve cells of a species of these see-through animals. Unlike flatworms, these animals have a complete digestive tract, with food entering the mouth and wastes leaving through a separate opening.
tossups.r: Most have thread-shaped bodies tapered at both ends. For 10 points, name this phylum of unsegmented worms that includes _C. elegans_.

tossups.p: In 2023, scientists reported reviving tiny members of this phylum that had been frozen in Siberian permafrost for more than 40,000 years. Despite its name, the skin infection ringworm is caused by a fungus, not by one of these animals.
tossups.r: Mosquitoes spread one of these animals, the heartworm, to dogs. For 10 points, name this phylum of worms that also includes hookworms and pinworms.

clues.t: A phylum of smooth, unsegmented worms with cylindrical bodies tapered at both ends
Parasitic members include hookworms, pinworms, and the heartworms that mosquitoes spread to dogs
The tiny see-through soil worm _Caenorhabditis elegans_ (_C. elegans_) is a famous laboratory model organism
Found in soil, in oceans, and inside plants and animals; they may be the most numerous animals on Earth
Covered by a tough outer cuticle that they shed (molt) as they grow, which puts them in the group Ecdysozoa with arthropods
Their fluid-filled body cavity, a pseudocoelom, is only partly lined by mesoderm, so they are called pseudocoelomates
Unlike flatworms, they have a complete digestive tract with two openings: a mouth at one end and an anus at the other
Have only lengthwise (longitudinal) muscles, so they move by whipping back and forth; they have no circulatory or respiratory system
Their name comes from the Greek word for “thread”
Adult _C. elegans_ hermaphrodites have exactly 959 body cells, including 302 nerve cells
_Ascaris_ causes one of the most common worm infections in the world and can grow longer than a foot
Mosquito-borne filarial worms cause elephantiasis (lymphatic filariasis), severe swelling, often of the legs
Victor Ambros and Gary Ruvkun won the 2024 Nobel Prize for discovering microRNAs, starting with lin-4, in _C. elegans_
Andrew Fire and Craig Mello won the 2006 Nobel Prize for RNA interference, found by injecting double-stranded RNA into _C. elegans_
John Sulston mapped the complete cell lineage of _C. elegans_, in which 131 cells die by programmed cell death; he shared the 2002 Nobel Prize with Sydney Brenner and H. Robert Horvitz
_C. elegans_ had the first complete wiring diagram of an animal’s nervous system (1986) and the first fully sequenced animal genome (1998)
_C. elegans_ worms survived the 2003 _Columbia_ space shuttle disaster and were found alive in the wreckage
Cynthia Kenyon doubled the lifespan of _C. elegans_ with a change in the gene daf-2; hungry larvae can enter a tough “dauer” (German for “lasting”) stage
Martin Chalfie made green fluorescent protein glow in the nerve cells of _C. elegans_ and shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
The “devil worm,” _Halicephalobus mephisto_, lives over a kilometer underground in a South African gold mine; Nathan Cobb wrote that a film of them would still outline Earth’s landscape
William Campbell and Satoshi Ōmura won the 2015 Nobel Prize for avermectin; the drug ivermectin fights river blindness, which black flies spread
The Carter Center’s campaign cut Guinea worm disease from about 3.5 million cases (1986) to fewer than 30 a year in the 2020s; people catch it from water fleas in drinking water
John D. Rockefeller funded a 1909 campaign against hookworm in the American South; hookworm larvae enter through bare feet, and the genus name _Necator_ means “killer”
_Trichinella_ worms cause trichinosis, caught from undercooked pork or wild game; their larvae curl up in tiny cysts in muscle
Root-knot species cause galls on plant roots, the soybean cyst species is a major U.S. crop pest, and marigold roots release chemicals toxic to them
In 2023, scientists revived some that had been frozen in Siberian permafrost for over 40,000 years; ringworm, despite its name, is a fungus, not one of them

trap.title: Roundworms, flatworms, or annelids?
trap.body: Three phyla of worms show up in quiz bowl, and tossups on nematodes often name one of the others to rule it out. Flatworms (Platyhelminthes), like tapeworms and planarians, are flat and lack a gut with two openings, while annelids, like earthworms and leeches, are built from ring-shaped segments. Players also mix up nematodes with nematocysts, the stinging cells of jellyfish, and with ringworm, which is a fungus.
trap.fix: Unsegmented, cylindrical bodies, a pseudocoelom, a gut with two openings, molting, hookworms, or _C. elegans_ mean nematodes (roundworms). Flat bodies or tapeworms mean flatworms; ring-shaped segments, earthworms, or leeches mean annelids.
trap.line: Real answer line: Nematodes (accept roundworms or Nematoda; prompt on worms; do not accept “flatworms” or “annelids”)

topics.name: Platelets
topics.kicker: Tiny cell fragments in the blood · Plug leaks and help clots form
topics.dates: Each one lasts about 7 to 10 days
topics.briefing: Platelets are tiny, colorless pieces of cells, and a single drop of your blood holds millions of them, waiting for a leak. When a blood vessel is cut, they stick to the damaged wall, turn spiky, and clump into a plug, then help the clotting process seal the wound. Each one breaks off from a giant cell in the bone marrow, has no nucleus, and lasts only about 7 to 10 days.
topics.answerHtml: Platelets (accept thrombocytes; prompt on blood cells; do not accept “red blood cells,” “white blood cells,” or “clotting factors”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1882, Italian doctor Giulio Bizzozero showed that these structures pile up at damaged blood vessels and help form clots, and he called them “little plates.” When resting, these colorless structures are flat, smooth discs about one-third the width of a red blood cell.
tossups.r: They have no nucleus and are made in the bone marrow. For 10 points, name these cell fragments that help blood clot.

tossups.p: In 1906, James Homer Wright showed that these structures come from megakaryocytes [“meg-uh-KAIR-ee-oh-sites”], giant bone marrow cells whose nuclei hold many copies of their DNA. Each megakaryocyte stretches long arms into blood vessels and sheds thousands of these structures.
tossups.r: These structures gather at cuts to plug leaks in blood vessels. For 10 points, name these tiny cell fragments that help blood clot.

tossups.p: Aspirin makes these structures less sticky for their whole lifespan, because it permanently blocks their cyclooxygenase [“sy-kloh-OK-sih-juh-nayss”] enzyme, and they have no nucleus with which to make more. Without that enzyme, they cannot make thromboxane [“THROM-bok-sayn”], a signal that calls more of them to a wound.
tossups.r: Each one lasts only about 7 to 10 days. For 10 points, name these blood cell fragments that clump together to stop bleeding.

tossups.p: Healthy blood vessel walls release prostacyclin [“pros-tuh-SY-klin”], which keeps these structures from sticking where they are not needed. When these structures are activated, they release ADP and thromboxane, which recruit even more of them in a classic example of positive feedback.
tossups.r: They then clump together into a plug at a wound. For 10 points, name these cell fragments that help blood clot.

tossups.p: A large protein called von Willebrand factor acts like glue that lets these structures stick to collagen exposed in a damaged blood vessel wall. Too little of that protein causes von Willebrand disease, the most common inherited bleeding disorder.
tossups.r: After sticking, these structures turn spiky and clump together. For 10 points, name these cell fragments that help seal wounds.

tossups.p: The liver makes a hormone called thrombopoietin [“throm-boh-POY-ih-tin”], which tells the bone marrow how many of these structures to produce. A count below about 150,000 of these structures per microliter of blood is called thrombocytopenia [“throm-boh-sy-toh-PEE-nee-uh”], which can cause easy bruising.
tossups.r: These structures have no nucleus. For 10 points, name these cell fragments, made from megakaryocytes, that help blood clot.

tossups.p: Unlike donated red blood cells, which are refrigerated, donations of these structures must be kept at room temperature and gently shaken, and they last only about five to seven days. Donors can give them through apheresis [“af-uh-REE-sis”], in which a machine collects these structures and returns the rest of the blood.
tossups.r: These structures gather at wounds to help form clots. For 10 points, name these colorless cell fragments found in blood.

tossups.p: These structures carry most of the serotonin in the bloodstream, soaking it up from the plasma and storing it in dense granules along with calcium and ADP. Their alpha granules hold a growth factor named for them that helps wounds heal.
tossups.r: They form plugs that stop bleeding at wounds. For 10 points, name these cell fragments made in the bone marrow.

tossups.p: Birds, reptiles, and fish lack these structures; instead, they use complete cells that still have a nucleus to do the same job in clotting. In mammals, these structures are fragments pinched off from giant cells in the bone marrow.
tossups.r: They last only about 7 to 10 days in the blood. For 10 points, name these tiny pieces of cells that plug leaks in blood vessels.

tossups.p: When these structures are activated, a receptor on their surface called glycoprotein IIb/IIIa [“two-B three-A”] grabs fibrinogen, which links neighboring ones together. Activation also changes them from smooth discs into spiky, spread-out shapes with long, finger-like projections.
tossups.r: Threads of fibrin then strengthen the plug they form at a wound. For 10 points, name these cell fragments that help blood clot.

tossups.p: In primary hemostasis [“hee-moh-STAY-sis”], these structures form a loose plug after a blood vessel narrows in a step called vascular spasm. In secondary hemostasis, a cascade of clotting factors ends when the enzyme thrombin turns fibrinogen into fibrin threads that hold their plug in place.
tossups.r: They have no nucleus. For 10 points, name these cell fragments that gather at cuts to help stop bleeding.

tossups.p: About one-third of these structures are held in reserve in the spleen at any moment. When these structures clump together inside an artery instead of at a wound, the clot they help form can block blood flow and cause a heart attack or a stroke.
tossups.r: Normally, they help stop bleeding at cuts. For 10 points, name these cell fragments made from megakaryocytes.

tossups.p: These structures are the smallest of the three main formed elements of blood, at only about 2 to 3 micrometers across. A normal count of them is about 150,000 to 450,000 per microliter of blood.
tossups.r: Unlike red and white blood cells, they are only fragments of cells. For 10 points, name these blood components that help form clots.

tossups.p: These structures, which develop from the myeloid [“MY-uh-loyd”] line of blood stem cells, have another name that comes from Greek words meaning “clot cell.” Despite that name, they are not true cells, since each one is a small, nucleus-free piece of a much larger cell.
tossups.r: Their numbers are checked in a complete blood count. For 10 points, name these blood components that clump together to stop bleeding.

tossups.p: Using the proteins actin and myosin, these structures pull on fibrin threads to tighten a clot, a process called clot retraction. They bud off from giant bone marrow cells whose name means “big nucleus cells.”
tossups.r: They have no nucleus of their own. For 10 points, name these cell fragments that help blood clot and plug leaks in blood vessels.

At a cut, they stick to the damaged blood vessel wall and form a plug

Have no nucleus, since each one is only a piece of a cell

Pinched off from giant bone marrow cells called megakaryocytes (“big nucleus cells”); each one sheds thousands
Each one lasts about 7 to 10 days; the spleen removes old ones and holds about a third of them in reserve

Giulio Bizzozero showed in 1882 that they help form clots, and he called them “little plates”

The liver makes thrombopoietin, the hormone that controls how many of them the bone marrow produces

Their other name comes from Greek words meaning “clot cell”; they come from the myeloid line of blood stem cells

trap.title: Cells, fragments, or factors?
trap.body: Platelets show up in tossups about blood, clotting, and bone marrow, so players often blurt “red blood cells” or “white blood cells” as soon as they hear “made in the bone marrow.” Others answer “fibrin” or “clotting factors,” which are proteins dissolved in the plasma, not the cell pieces themselves. Hemophilia, for example, comes from missing clotting factors, not from missing platelets.
trap.fix: Cell fragments with no nucleus, megakaryocytes, a plug at a wound, aspirin, or von Willebrand factor mean platelets (or thrombocytes). Thrombin, fibrin threads, or vitamin K point to clotting proteins; oxygen and hemoglobin mean red blood cells.
trap.line: Real answer line: Platelets (accept thrombocytes; prompt on blood cells; do not accept “red blood cells,” “white blood cells,” or “clotting factors”)

topics.name: Yeast
topics.kicker: Single-celled fungi · Make bread rise by fermenting sugar
topics.briefing: Yeasts are single-celled fungi, and one species, baker’s yeast, has helped people make bread for thousands of years. When yeast cells ferment sugar without oxygen, they release carbon dioxide gas, which puffs up bread dough, along with ethanol. Because they are simple, fast-growing cells with a nucleus like ours, yeasts are also favorite lab organisms, and research on them has won several Nobel Prizes.
topics.answerHtml: Yeast (accept yeasts, Saccharomyces, or Saccharomyces cerevisiae; accept baker’s yeast or brewer’s yeast; prompt on fungi or fungus; do not accept “mold” or “bacteria”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Yoshinori Ohsumi won the 2016 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for using these organisms to work out how autophagy [“aw-TOFF-uh-jee”] works, the process by which cells break down and recycle their own parts. Roger Kornberg won a 2006 Nobel Prize for showing, with an enzyme from these organisms, how cells copy DNA into RNA.
tossups.r: In 1996, the baker’s species became the first eukaryote with a fully sequenced genome. For 10 points, name these single-celled fungi.

tossups.p: Paul Nurse shared the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for finding the gene cdc2, which controls cell division, in a species of these organisms that divides by splitting in two. That species’ name, pombe, comes from a Swahili word for beer.
tossups.r: A more common species of these organisms reproduces by budding and is used to make bread. For 10 points, name these single-celled fungi.

tossups.p: Randy Schekman shared a 2013 Nobel Prize for studying mutant cells of these organisms that could not ship proteins out properly, revealing genes that control how tiny bubbles called vesicles move cargo. Leland Hartwell shared a 2001 Nobel Prize for finding “cell division cycle” genes in the same kind of organism.
tossups.r: Many of these organisms reproduce by budding. For 10 points, name these single-celled fungi that make bread rise.

tossups.p: Eduard Buchner won the 1907 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for showing that juice squeezed from ground-up cells of these organisms could still ferment sugar, even though the cells were dead. Wilhelm Kühne [“KOO-nuh”] coined the word “enzyme” from Greek words meaning “in leaven,” referring to these organisms.
tossups.r: During fermentation, these organisms turn sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide. For 10 points, name these single-celled fungi.

tossups.p: Justus von Liebig [“LEE-big”] argued that fermentation was a purely chemical process, but Louis Pasteur showed that it is carried out by these living organisms. An effect named for Pasteur describes how oxygen slows down fermentation by these organisms, which can switch to aerobic respiration when oxygen is present.
tossups.r: Without oxygen, they turn sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide. For 10 points, name these single-celled fungi used in baking and brewing.

tossups.p: In 1883, Emil Christian Hansen of the Carlsberg Laboratory in Copenhagen grew a pure culture from a single cell of these organisms, so brewers could stop wild strains from spoiling their batches. A species he studied was long named for that Danish brewery.
tossups.r: Louis Pasteur showed that these living organisms cause fermentation. For 10 points, name these single-celled fungi that reproduce by budding.

tossups.p: Cells of these organisms come in two mating types, called a and alpha, which signal each other with pheromones. When a cell senses the opposite type, it grows a projection nicknamed a “shmoo,” after a cartoon creature from the comic strip _Li’l Abner_.
tossups.r: These organisms usually reproduce by budding. For 10 points, name these single-celled fungi that make bread rise.

tossups.p: Each time a mother cell of these organisms produces a daughter, it is left with a ring-shaped scar rich in chitin [“KYE-tin”], so counting those scars shows how many daughters it has made. Each daughter grows as a small bulge on the mother cell before pinching off.
tossups.r: This kind of reproduction is called budding. For 10 points, name these single-celled fungi that release carbon dioxide to make bread rise.

tossups.p: Under stress, cells of the baker’s species of these organisms can undergo meiosis and form four spores inside a sac called an ascus [“AS-kus”], so that species is classified as a sac fungus. Their cell walls are built mostly from sugar chains called glucans, with a smaller amount of chitin.
tossups.r: Bakers often buy them as dry granules in small packets. For 10 points, name these single-celled fungi that make bread dough rise.

tossups.p: In 1986, a vaccine against hepatitis B became the first vaccine made with recombinant DNA, after scientists inserted a viral gene into these organisms so they would produce a harmless viral protein. Some insulin for people with diabetes is also made by genetically engineered cells of these organisms.
tossups.r: Like human cells, they are eukaryotes with a nucleus. For 10 points, name these single-celled fungi used in baking.

tossups.p: Marmite, first made in 1902 in the English brewing town of Burton upon Trent, and Australia’s Vegemite are salty spreads made from extracts of these organisms left over from brewing. A flaky, deactivated form of these organisms is sold as a cheesy-tasting topping.
tossups.r: They give off carbon dioxide gas. For 10 points, name these single-celled fungi that bakers use to make bread dough rise.

tossups.p: The scientific name of the most familiar species of these organisms comes from Greek and Latin words meaning “sugar fungus” and “of beer.” Ancient Egyptians used these organisms to make bread thousands of years ago.
tossups.r: Jewish families eat matzah, a flat bread made without them or any other leavening, during Passover. For 10 points, name these single-celled fungi.

tossups.p: Most of the ethanol blended into American gasoline is made when these organisms ferment sugars from corn. In a kitchen, the gas they release gets trapped in a stretchy protein network called gluten, while the ethanol they make mostly evaporates in the oven.
tossups.r: That gas, carbon dioxide, makes bread dough rise. For 10 points, name these single-celled fungi used in baking.

tossups.p: Arthur Harden and Hans von Euler-Chelpin shared the 1929 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for studying how extracts of these organisms ferment sugar. In 1965, Robert Holley worked out the full sequence of a transfer RNA molecule taken from these organisms.
tossups.r: These organisms are fungi that usually reproduce by budding. For 10 points, name these single-celled organisms that make bread rise.

tossups.p: In a two-hybrid screen, invented by Stanley Fields in 1989, scientists test whether two proteins stick together by checking whether they switch on a reporter gene inside cells of these organisms. The baker’s species of these organisms has 16 chromosomes and about 6,000 genes.
tossups.r: Wild ones in a sourdough starter work alongside lactic acid bacteria. For 10 points, name these single-celled fungi that make bread rise.

trap.title: Organism, kingdom, or process?
trap.body: Tossups on yeast keep mentioning fermentation, bread, and the kingdom Fungi, so players buzz with “fermentation” (the process), “fungi” (the whole kingdom, which only earns a prompt), or “mold.” Others confuse yeast with the bacteria used to make yogurt, or with baking soda, a chemical that also makes baked goods rise.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “these organisms” or “these single-celled fungi” that bud, make bread rise, or turn sugar into ethanol, say yeast. Say fermentation only for “this process,” and say fungi only if the question asks for the whole kingdom.
trap.line: Real answer line: Yeast (accept Saccharomyces; accept baker’s yeast or brewer’s yeast; prompt on fungi; do not accept “mold” or “bacteria”)

topics.name: Sickle-cell disease
topics.kicker: Inherited hemoglobin disorder · Red blood cells can bend into crescents
topics.dates: First described in Western medicine in 1910
topics.briefing: Sickle-cell disease is an inherited blood disorder caused by a tiny change in the gene for hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells. In people with the disease, red blood cells can stiffen into crescent, or sickle, shapes that get stuck in small blood vessels and wear out quickly. Carrying just one copy of the gene gives some protection against malaria, which is why it is most common in families with roots in sub-Saharan Africa, India, the Mediterranean, and the Middle East.
topics.answerHtml: Sickle-cell disease (accept sickle-cell anemia or SCD; prompt on anemia; do not accept “sickle-cell trait,” “malaria,” or “hemoglobin”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1910, Chicago doctor James Herrick published the first Western medical description of this condition, after his intern Ernest Irons saw strangely elongated red blood cells in a blood sample from a dental student from Grenada named Walter Clement Noel.
tossups.r: In this disorder, red blood cells can bend into crescent shapes. For 10 points, name this inherited blood disorder.

tossups.p: In 1949, Linus Pauling’s team, including Harvey Itano [“ih-TAH-noh”], used electrophoresis, which separates molecules in an electric field, to show that the hemoglobin of people with this condition carries a different electric charge than normal hemoglobin. Their paper called this condition a “molecular disease,” the first ever identified.
tossups.r: It is caused by an altered form of hemoglobin. For 10 points, name this inherited blood disorder.

tossups.p: In the 1950s, Vernon Ingram chopped normal and abnormal hemoglobin into pieces and compared their “fingerprints,” finding that the hemoglobin in this condition differs by just one amino acid in each beta chain: valine replaces glutamic acid.
tossups.r: That change can make red blood cells bend into stiff crescent shapes. For 10 points, name this inherited blood disorder.

tossups.p: In 1954, Anthony Allison showed that children in East Africa who carried one copy of the gene for this condition had fewer heavy malaria infections, and he noted that the gene was most common where malaria was widespread.
tossups.r: That protection is a classic example of heterozygote advantage. For 10 points, name this inherited blood disorder caused by a change in hemoglobin.

tossups.p: In 2019, Victoria Gray of Mississippi became the first person in the United States treated for this condition with CRISPR gene editing. In 2023, that therapy, Casgevy, became the first approved medicine based on CRISPR; it edits a patient’s blood stem cells so that their red blood cells make fetal hemoglobin.
tossups.r: This condition is caused by a change in hemoglobin. For 10 points, name this inherited disorder in which red blood cells can bend into crescent shapes.

tossups.p: The mutation behind this condition changes a single DNA letter, turning the codon GAG into GTG, a classic example of a missense point mutation. The changed gene, HBB, sits on chromosome 11 and codes for the beta chain of an oxygen-carrying protein.
tossups.r: That change puts valine in place of glutamic acid. For 10 points, name this inherited blood disorder in which red blood cells can become crescent-shaped.

tossups.p: When oxygen levels drop, the hemoglobin molecules in this condition stick together into long, stiff fibers, because the nonpolar amino acid valine fits into a water-fearing pocket on a neighboring molecule. Those fibers distort the red blood cells that hold them.
tossups.r: The stiff cells can then get stuck in small blood vessels. For 10 points, name this inherited blood disorder caused by hemoglobin S.

tossups.p: Babies with this condition usually show no signs of it for their first several months, because their red blood cells are still full of fetal hemoglobin. The drug hydroxyurea [“hy-DROK-see-yoo-REE-uh”] is used to treat this condition because it raises fetal hemoglobin levels.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this inherited blood disorder in which red blood cells can become stiff and crescent-shaped.

tossups.p: People who inherit hemoglobin S from one parent and hemoglobin C from the other have a usually milder form of this condition called HbSC disease. This condition is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, so two carrier parents have a one-in-four chance of passing it to each child.
tossups.r: Carriers usually have no symptoms. For 10 points, name this inherited blood disorder caused by a change in hemoglobin.

tossups.p: The United Nations recognized this condition as a public health problem in 2008, and June 19 has since been marked as a world awareness day for it. In the United States, September is national awareness month for this condition, which affects about 100,000 Americans.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this inherited blood disorder in which red blood cells can take on a crescent shape.

tossups.p: In 1972, President Richard Nixon signed a national act to fund screening, research, and treatment programs for this condition. All U.S. states test newborn babies for it, often with a blood test that separates different forms of hemoglobin.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this inherited blood disorder in which hemoglobin S can make red blood cells stiff and crescent-shaped.

tossups.p: Red blood cells in this condition may last only 10 to 20 days instead of the usual 120, which leads to a shortage of red blood cells called anemia. Stiff cells can also block small blood vessels, causing sudden episodes of pain called crises.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this inherited blood disorder in which red blood cells can bend into crescent shapes.

tossups.p: This condition is most common among people whose ancestors came from sub-Saharan Africa, India, the Mediterranean, and the Middle East, regions where malaria has long been common. It is the most common inherited blood disorder in the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disorder in which red blood cells can bend into crescent shapes.

tossups.p: Biologists write the protein change behind this condition as E6V, since the amino acid valine, abbreviated V, replaces glutamic acid, abbreviated E, at the sixth position of hemoglobin’s beta chain. Because valine is nonpolar and glutamic acid is charged, the change makes the protein less soluble when it lacks oxygen.
tossups.r: This condition is named for the curved farm tool that affected red blood cells can resemble. For 10 points, name this inherited blood disorder.

tossups.p: Biology textbooks use this condition as a classic example of balancing selection, since the gene that causes it stays common even though people who inherit two copies have serious health problems. One copy helps protect against severe malaria caused by _Plasmodium falciparum_ [“fal-SIP-uh-rum”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this inherited disorder in which red blood cells can become crescent-shaped.

trap.title: Disease, trait, or malaria?
trap.body: These tossups are full of clues about hemoglobin, red blood cells, and malaria, and each of those is its own answer line, so blurting the protein, the cells, or the mosquito-borne disease loses the question. Another trap is sickle-cell trait, the carrier condition: people with only one copy of the gene usually have no symptoms, so the trait is not the same thing as the disease.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this disease” or “this disorder” in which red blood cells bend into crescents, say sickle-cell disease (sickle-cell anemia is also fine). Say hemoglobin only for “this protein,” red blood cells for “these cells,” and malaria for a disease spread by mosquitoes.
trap.line: Real answer line: Sickle-cell disease (accept sickle-cell anemia or SCD; prompt on anemia; do not accept “sickle-cell trait,” “malaria,” or “hemoglobin”)

topics.name: Cartilage
topics.kicker: Flexible connective tissue · Shapes ears and noses and cushions joints
topics.dates: Forms most of an embryo’s early skeleton
topics.briefing: Cartilage is the firm but bendable tissue that gives shape to your outer ears and the tip of your nose and keeps your windpipe open. A smooth layer of it covers the ends of bones in joints, so they glide instead of grinding. Cartilage has no blood vessels, so it heals slowly, and sharks and rays have skeletons made almost entirely of it.
topics.answerHtml: Cartilage (accept specific types such as hyaline cartilage, elastic cartilage, or fibrocartilage; accept gristle; prompt on connective tissue; do not accept “bone,” “ligaments,” or “collagen”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Tiny mineral tiles called tesserae [“TESS-uh-ree”] reinforce this tissue in the skeletons of one class of fish. That class, Chondrichthyes [“kon-DRIK-thee-eez”], is named from Greek words for this tissue and “fish,” since its members have skeletons made of this tissue instead of bone.
tossups.r: That class includes sharks and rays. For 10 points, name this flexible connective tissue that also shapes the human nose and ears.

tossups.p: The largest piece of this tissue in the voice box, whose Greek-based name means “shield-shaped,” forms the bump called the Adam’s apple. A ring of this tissue called the cricoid [“KRY-koyd”] sits just below it, at the top of the windpipe.
tossups.r: C-shaped rings of this tissue hold the windpipe open. For 10 points, name this flexible connective tissue.

tossups.p: The elastic type of this tissue, which gets its springiness from a protein called elastin, supports the epiglottis [“ep-ih-GLOT-iss”], the flap that covers the windpipe when a person swallows. That type is also found in the tube that connects the middle ear to the throat.
tossups.r: It also gives shape to the outer ear. For 10 points, name this flexible connective tissue.

tossups.p: The most common type of this tissue is called hyaline [“HY-uh-lin”], from a Greek word for “glass,” because it looks smooth and glassy, and its matrix is rich in type II collagen. Most of an embryo’s skeleton first forms as models made of that type, which are later replaced by bone.
tossups.r: A smooth layer of it covers the ends of bones in joints. For 10 points, name this flexible connective tissue.

tossups.p: The toughest type of this tissue contains thick bundles of type I collagen and forms the outer rings of the discs between vertebrae. That fibrous type also makes up the crescent-shaped pads called menisci [“meh-NISS-kye”] that cushion each knee.
tossups.r: Tearing one of those pads is a common sports injury. For 10 points, name this flexible connective tissue that also shapes the nose and outer ear.

tossups.p: Most of this tissue is wrapped in a dense layer called the perichondrium [“pair-ih-KON-dree-um”], which supplies it with nutrients and new cells. This tissue has no blood vessels or nerves, so nutrients must diffuse through it, which is one reason injuries to it heal slowly.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this flexible connective tissue that covers the ends of bones in joints.

tossups.p: Cells called chondrocytes [“KON-droh-sites”] live in small spaces called lacunae [“luh-KOO-nee”] inside this tissue, surrounded by a matrix they make. That matrix is packed with water-holding molecules such as aggrecan [“AG-ruh-kan”] and chondroitin [“kon-DROY-tin”] sulfate, which help this tissue resist being squeezed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this flexible connective tissue that shapes the outer ear and the tip of the nose.

tossups.p: In endochondral [“en-doh-KON-drul”] ossification, a model made of this tissue is gradually replaced by bone. Long bones grow longer at growth plates, also called epiphyseal [“ep-ih-FIZ-ee-ul”] plates, which are made of this tissue and turn into bone after puberty.
tossups.r: This tissue also shapes the nose and outer ear. For 10 points, name this flexible connective tissue that cushions joints.

tossups.p: Achondroplasia [“ay-kon-droh-PLAY-zhuh”], the most common cause of dwarfism, results from a change in the gene FGFR3 that slows the growth of this tissue in the growth plates of long bones. The condition’s name comes from Greek words meaning “without formation” of this tissue.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this flexible connective tissue that covers the ends of bones in joints.

tossups.p: In synovial [“sih-NOH-vee-ul”] joints, a slippery fluid containing hyaluronic [“hy-uh-loo-RON-ik”] acid and a protein called lubricin keeps the smooth articular type of this tissue gliding with very little friction. Because this tissue lacks blood vessels, damage to it in a knee or hip heals poorly.
tossups.r: Its gradual wearing away causes osteoarthritis. For 10 points, name this flexible connective tissue that also shapes the ear and nose.

tossups.p: This tissue can grow in two ways: interstitial growth, in which cells inside it divide and add matrix from within, and appositional growth, in which cells called chondroblasts in its outer covering add new layers to its surface.
tossups.r: Unlike bone, it has no blood vessels. For 10 points, name this flexible tissue that forms C-shaped rings in the windpipe.

tossups.p: Flexible bars of this tissue connect the upper ten pairs of ribs, directly or indirectly, to the breastbone, letting the chest expand during breathing. About 16 to 20 C-shaped rings of this tissue keep the trachea from collapsing.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this flexible connective tissue that shapes the outer ear and the tip of the nose.

tossups.p: Lampreys and hagfish, which are jawless fish, have skeletons made mostly of this tissue rather than bone. Medical words that begin with “chondro-,” such as chondrocyte and chondroitin, come from the Greek word for this tissue.
tossups.r: Sharks also have skeletons made of it. For 10 points, name this flexible tissue found in the human nose and outer ear.

tossups.p: The rings of this tissue in the trachea are open at the back, where the trachealis [“tray-kee-AL-iss”] muscle lets the esophagus bulge forward as food is swallowed. Smaller plates of this tissue support the bronchi, but the narrower bronchioles lack it.
tossups.r: This tissue is firm but bendable, like the tip of your nose. For 10 points, name this connective tissue that cushions the ends of bones in joints.

tossups.p: In 1743, Scottish anatomist William Hunter observed that once this tissue in a joint is destroyed, it does not grow back. Unlike bone, its matrix is normally not hardened by calcium phosphate crystals, so it stays firm but bendable.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this connective tissue that shapes the nose and outer ear and makes up a shark’s skeleton.

In shark skeletons it is strengthened by tiny mineral tiles called tesserae
The class Chondrichthyes (sharks, skates, and rays) is named from Greek words for it and “fish”; words starting with “chondro-” refer to it
The ring-shaped cricoid sits just below the Adam’s apple, at the top of the windpipe
The elastic type gets its spring from elastin and supports the epiglottis, the outer ear, and the tube from the middle ear to the throat
Hyaline comes from a Greek word for “glass”; the hyaline type’s matrix is rich in type II collagen
The fibrous type contains thick bundles of type I collagen, which makes it the toughest type
Most of it is wrapped in a dense layer called the perichondrium, which supplies nutrients and new cells
Its matrix holds water-loving aggrecan and chondroitin sulfate, which help it resist being squeezed
Grows in two ways: interstitial (cells divide from within) and appositional (chondroblasts add layers at the surface)

Synovial fluid with hyaluronic acid and lubricin keeps the smooth articular type gliding with very little friction
