trap.title: Not bone, not ligament
trap.body: Cartilage tossups describe joints, ribs, and skeletons, so players often blurt “bone,” or they name ligaments and tendons, the tough cords that connect bone to bone and muscle to bone. Others hear “collagen” or “chondrocytes” and name one ingredient of the tissue instead of the tissue itself, or say “joint” when the question asks what covers the ends of the bones.
trap.fix: Flexible, no blood vessels, chondrocytes in lacunae, the epiglottis, the Adam’s apple, shark skeletons, or growth plates mean cartilage. Cords that connect bones mean ligaments, cords from muscle to bone mean tendons, and a hard, mineral-filled tissue with marrow means bone.
trap.line: Real answer line: Cartilage (accept hyaline cartilage, elastic cartilage, or fibrocartilage; prompt on connective tissue; do not accept “bone,” “ligaments,” or “collagen”)

topics.name: Pituitary gland
topics.kicker: Pea-sized gland under the brain · Nicknamed the “master gland”
topics.dates: Weighs only about half a gram
topics.briefing: The pituitary gland is a pea-sized gland that hangs from the underside of the brain, tucked into a bony pocket in the skull. It is nicknamed the “master gland” because its hormones tell other glands, like the thyroid and adrenal glands, what to do, and it also makes growth hormone. But the pituitary has a boss of its own: the hypothalamus, the brain region just above it.
topics.answerHtml: Pituitary gland (accept hypophysis; prompt on master gland; do not accept “hypothalamus” or “pineal gland”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This gland’s name comes from the Latin word for “phlegm” or “slime,” because ancient physicians such as Galen believed that it drained mucus from the brain into the nose. It sits in a saddle-shaped hollow of the sphenoid [“SFEE-noyd”] bone called the sella turcica [“SEL-uh TUR-sih-kuh”], or “Turkish saddle.”
tossups.r: It hangs from the hypothalamus by a thin stalk. For 10 points, name this pea-sized “master gland” at the base of the brain.

tossups.p: Harvey Cushing, often called the father of modern neurosurgery, described a disease in which a tumor in this gland releases too much ACTH, causing the adrenal glands to make too much cortisol. His 1912 book was devoted to this gland and its disorders.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gland at the base of the brain that is controlled by the hypothalamus.

tossups.p: Robert Wadlow, the tallest person in recorded history at 8 feet 11 inches, grew so tall because this gland of his released far too much of a growth-promoting hormone. In adults, too much of that hormone causes acromegaly [“ak-roh-MEG-uh-lee”], in which the hands, feet, and jaw slowly enlarge.
tossups.r: That hormone is growth hormone. For 10 points, name this pea-sized gland at the base of the brain.

tossups.p: Argentine scientist Bernardo Houssay [“oo-SY”] shared the 1947 Nobel Prize for showing that hormones from the front lobe of this gland affect how the body handles sugar. He was the first Latin American to win a Nobel Prize in a science.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gland at the base of the brain, nicknamed the “master gland.”

tossups.p: Roger Guillemin [“gee-yuh-MAN”] and Andrew Schally shared a 1977 Nobel Prize for identifying “releasing” hormones, such as TRH, that the hypothalamus sends to this gland through a tiny system of portal blood vessels. Geoffrey Harris had earlier shown that the hypothalamus controls this gland’s front lobe through those vessels.
tossups.r: It makes growth hormone. For 10 points, name this pea-sized gland, nicknamed the “master gland,” that hangs below the brain.

tossups.p: This gland sits just below the optic chiasm [“KY-az-um”], where the optic nerves cross, so a tumor growing upward from it can cause loss of side vision in both eyes. A thin stalk called the infundibulum [“in-fun-DIB-yoo-lum”] connects this gland to the brain.
tossups.r: It releases growth hormone. For 10 points, name this pea-sized “master gland” that hangs below the hypothalamus.

tossups.p: The back lobe of this gland is made of nerve tissue and does not make its own hormones; instead, it stores and releases oxytocin [“ok-sih-TOH-sin”] and vasopressin [“vay-zoh-PRESS-in”], which are made in the hypothalamus. Too little vasopressin from it causes diabetes insipidus, in which the kidneys release too much water.
tossups.r: It is nicknamed the “master gland.” For 10 points, name this pea-sized gland whose front lobe makes growth hormone.

tossups.p: This gland’s front lobe releases two gonadotropins [“go-nad-oh-TROH-pinz”], FSH and LH, which act on the ovaries and testes, as well as prolactin, which tells the body to make milk. Students remember that lobe’s six main hormones with the mnemonic “FLAT PeG.”
tossups.r: The G in that mnemonic stands for growth hormone. For 10 points, name this pea-sized gland below the hypothalamus.

tossups.p: Cells called thyrotropes [“THY-roh-trohps”] in this gland make thyroid-stimulating hormone, and they release less of it when thyroxine levels in the blood rise, a classic example of negative feedback. Other cells in this gland, called lactotropes, make prolactin.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gland at the base of the brain, nicknamed the “master gland.”

tossups.p: A large protein called POMC is cut up inside this gland to make several smaller signals, including ACTH, beta-endorphin, and melanocyte-stimulating hormone. In many animals, a middle section of this gland called the intermediate lobe releases that last hormone, which darkens skin.
tossups.r: It hangs just below the hypothalamus. For 10 points, name this pea-sized gland that also releases growth hormone.

tossups.p: When a person is stressed, the hypothalamus releases corticotropin-releasing hormone, which travels a short distance to this gland and makes it release ACTH. ACTH then travels to the adrenal glands, which respond by releasing cortisol.
tossups.r: That chain of signals is called the HPA axis. For 10 points, name this gland, nicknamed the “master gland.”

tossups.p: This gland releases much of its somatotropin [“soh-muh-toh-TROH-pin”] during the deepest stage of sleep, when slow delta waves appear on an EEG. Somatotropin tells the liver to make a growth factor called IGF-1, which helps bones and muscles grow.
tossups.r: Somatotropin is better known as growth hormone. For 10 points, name this pea-sized gland at the base of the brain.

tossups.p: French neurologist Pierre Marie named acromegaly in 1886, from Greek words meaning “large extremities,” and doctors later traced that condition to tumors of this gland. The wrestler André the Giant had acromegaly.
tossups.r: Those tumors release too much growth hormone. For 10 points, name this pea-sized gland at the base of the brain.

tossups.p: The front lobe of this gland develops in the embryo from an upward pouch of tissue from the roof of the mouth called Rathke’s [“RAHT-kuhz”] pouch, while its back lobe grows down from the brain. That is why the two lobes are made of very different kinds of tissue.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this two-lobed gland at the base of the brain, nicknamed the “master gland.”

tossups.p: Vincent du Vigneaud [“doo VEEN-yoh”] won the 1955 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for making a hormone released by this gland’s back lobe in the lab. That hormone, oxytocin, is a rare example of positive feedback, since the contractions it triggers during childbirth cause even more of it to be released.
tossups.r: This gland weighs only about half a gram. For 10 points, name this pea-sized gland that hangs below the hypothalamus.

clues.t: Nicknamed the “master gland” because its hormones control other glands
A pea-sized gland, weighing about half a gram, that hangs from the underside of the brain
Makes growth hormone (somatotropin), which helps children grow
Hangs by a thin stalk from the hypothalamus, which controls it
Has a front (anterior) lobe made of gland tissue and a back (posterior) lobe made of nerve tissue
The back lobe stores and releases oxytocin and vasopressin (ADH), which are made in the hypothalamus
The front lobe makes TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin, and growth hormone (remembered as “FLAT PeG”)
Rising thyroxine makes it release less thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), a classic case of negative feedback
Its ACTH tells the adrenal glands to make cortisol, part of the stress response called the HPA axis
Too much growth hormone causes gigantism in children (as with Robert Wadlow) and acromegaly in adults
Releases much of its growth hormone during deep, slow-wave sleep; growth hormone tells the liver to make IGF-1
Too little vasopressin from it causes diabetes insipidus, in which the kidneys release too much water
Its name comes from the Latin word for “phlegm,” since Galen thought it drained mucus from the brain to the nose
Sits in the sella turcica (“Turkish saddle”), a hollow in the sphenoid bone
Harvey Cushing, the father of modern neurosurgery, described a disease in which a tumor here makes too much ACTH, raising cortisol
Bernardo Houssay won the 1947 Nobel Prize for showing that its front-lobe hormones affect sugar use; he was the first Latin American science Nobel winner
Roger Guillemin and Andrew Schally (1977 Nobel Prize) found the hypothalamus’s “releasing” hormones; Geoffrey Harris showed that they reach it through portal blood vessels
Sits just below the optic chiasm, so a tumor here can cause loss of side vision; a stalk called the infundibulum connects it to the brain
Its gonadotropins, FSH and LH, act on the ovaries and testes; its prolactin tells the body to make milk
Its cell types are named for what they make: thyrotropes make TSH and lactotropes make prolactin
POMC is cut up inside it into ACTH, beta-endorphin, and melanocyte-stimulating hormone; in many animals an intermediate lobe releases that last one
Pierre Marie named acromegaly (“large extremities”) in 1886; the wrestler André the Giant had it
Its front lobe develops from Rathke’s pouch in the roof of the embryo’s mouth, while its back lobe grows down from the brain
Vincent du Vigneaud won the 1955 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for making oxytocin in the lab; oxytocin shows positive feedback during childbirth

trap.title: Pituitary or hypothalamus?
trap.body: The pituitary and the hypothalamus work as a team, so tossups describe both: the hypothalamus sends “releasing” hormones down to the pituitary and makes the oxytocin and vasopressin that the pituitary’s back lobe stores. Players also confuse the pituitary with the pineal gland, a different small gland in the brain that makes melatonin, and with the thyroid, which the pituitary controls.
trap.fix: “This gland” that is pea-sized, sits in the sella turcica, makes growth hormone, TSH, or ACTH, or is called the “master gland” means the pituitary. “This brain region” that sends releasing hormones means the hypothalamus, and melatonin or sleep cycles mean the pineal gland.
trap.line: Real answer line: Pituitary gland (accept hypophysis; prompt on master gland; do not accept “hypothalamus” or “pineal gland”)

topics.name: Neanderthals
topics.kicker: Extinct Ice Age humans of Europe and Asia · Some of their DNA lives on in us
topics.briefing: Neanderthals were close cousins of modern humans who lived in Europe and western Asia during the Ice Ages and died out about 40,000 years ago. They were short and stocky, built for the cold, and they made stone tools, controlled fire, hunted big game, and buried their dead. When early modern humans met them, the two groups sometimes had children together, so most people with ancestors from outside Africa carry a little Neanderthal DNA.
topics.answerHtml: Neanderthals (accept Neandertals, Homo neanderthalensis, or Homo sapiens neanderthalensis; prompt on hominins or archaic humans; do not accept “Denisovans” or “Cro-Magnons”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: These hominins are named for a German valley that honors a 17th-century preacher and hymn writer whose surname is a Greek form of “new man.” Quarry workers dug up the first recognized fossils of this group in that valley’s Feldhofer Cave in 1856.
tossups.r: They died out about 40,000 years ago. For 10 points, name these extinct, stocky human relatives who lived in Ice Age Europe.

tossups.p: In 1864, geologist William King gave these hominins their scientific name, making them the first extinct human group formally named from fossils. Schoolteacher Johann Carl Fuhlrott had recognized that bones found in 1856 were not those of a modern person.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these extinct Ice Age humans whose DNA survives in many modern people.

tossups.p: A child’s skull found at Engis, Belgium, in 1829 and a skull found at Forbes’ Quarry on Gibraltar in 1848 were the first fossils of these hominins ever found, though no one recognized them as such until later.
tossups.r: These hominins take their name from a German valley where bones were found in 1856. For 10 points, name these extinct, cold-adapted human relatives.

tossups.p: Rudolf Virchow argued that the odd features of the 1856 skeleton of one of these hominins came from disease, such as rickets, rather than from a different kind of human. Thomas Henry Huxley discussed the same skull in his 1863 book _Evidence as to Man’s Place in Nature_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these extinct human relatives who lived in Europe until about 40,000 years ago.

tossups.p: Marcellin Boule [“BOOL”] reconstructed an old man’s skeleton from La Chapelle-aux-Saints [“lah shah-PEL oh SAN”], France, to show these hominins as stooped and apelike, an image later blamed partly on that man’s arthritis. That skeleton was found in a grave in 1908.
tossups.r: They actually walked fully upright and were stocky and strong. For 10 points, name these extinct relatives of modern humans.

tossups.p: Svante Pääbo [“SVAHN-teh PAY-boh”] won the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on ancient DNA that included sequencing the genome of these hominins, first published in draft form in 2010. In 1997, his team read a stretch of their mitochondrial DNA from the original 1856 fossil.
tossups.r: Their genome showed that they had children with early modern humans. For 10 points, name these extinct human relatives from Ice Age Europe.

tossups.p: A bone fragment from a Siberian cave belonged to a girl nicknamed “Denny,” whose mother was one of these hominins and whose father was a Denisovan [“deh-NEE-soh-vun”]. The Denisovans, identified in 2010 from a finger bone found in that same cave, were these hominins’ closest known relatives.
tossups.r: They died out about 40,000 years ago. For 10 points, name these extinct, stocky hominins who lived in Europe and western Asia.

tossups.p: Most people whose ancestors lived outside Africa carry about 1 to 2 percent of their DNA from these hominins, because early modern humans had children with them after leaving Africa. Some of the genes inherited from them affect the immune system and skin.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these extinct, cold-adapted human relatives whose fossils were first recognized in Germany in 1856.

tossups.p: These hominins made stone tools in the Mousterian [“moo-STEER-ee-un”] style, named for a site in France, often using the Levallois [“luh-val-WAH”] technique of shaping a stone core before striking off a flake. They also heated birch bark to make tar, a glue for attaching stone points to wooden handles.
tossups.r: They also controlled fire. For 10 points, name these extinct human relatives who lived in Europe and western Asia.

tossups.p: In the 1950s, Ralph Solecki [“soh-LEK-ee”] excavated Shanidar [“SHAH-nih-dar”] Cave in Iraq, where one skeleton of these hominins showed that the man had survived serious injuries for years, likely with help from his group. Solecki suggested that another burial there had been covered with flowers, an idea that later scientists questioned.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these extinct Ice Age hominins whose first recognized fossils were found in Germany.

tossups.p: A hyoid [“HY-oyd”] bone of one of these hominins, found at Kebara Cave in Israel, looks almost exactly like a modern human’s, which suggests they may have been able to speak. They also carried the same version of FOXP2, a gene linked to speech and language, as modern humans.
tossups.r: They died out about 40,000 years ago. For 10 points, name these extinct, big-brained human relatives who lived in Ice Age Europe.

tossups.p: Fossils about 430,000 years old from the Sima de los Huesos [“SEE-mah day lohs WAY-sohs”], or “Pit of Bones,” in Spain’s Atapuerca [“ah-tah-PWAIR-kah”] hills belong to early members of the line that led to these hominins. Many scientists think these hominins descended from a species called _Homo heidelbergensis_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these extinct, stocky human relatives who lived in Europe and western Asia.

tossups.p: William Golding’s 1955 novel _The Inheritors_ tells the story of a small band of these people, including Lok and Fa, as a newer kind of human arrives. In Jean M. Auel’s novel _The Clan of the Cave Bear_, a girl named Ayla is raised by a clan of these people.
tossups.r: Their first recognized fossils were found in Germany in 1856. For 10 points, name these extinct, stocky human relatives of Ice Age Europe.

tossups.p: Compared with modern humans, these hominins had a bulge at the back of the skull called an occipital [“ok-SIP-ih-tul”] bun, a large nose, and no true chin. Their brains were, on average, as large as or even larger than those of modern humans.
tossups.r: Their short, stocky bodies were built to hold in heat during the Ice Ages. For 10 points, name these extinct human relatives.

tossups.p: Some of the last of these hominins may have lived in Gorham’s Cave on Gibraltar, where crosshatched lines carved into the rock are thought to be their work. At Krapina, Croatia, they may have worn eagle talons as ornaments.
tossups.r: They died out about 40,000 years ago, not long after modern humans spread into Europe. For 10 points, name these extinct hominins named for a valley in Germany.

clues.t: Extinct close relatives of modern humans who lived in Europe and western Asia during the Ice Ages
Died out about 40,000 years ago, not long after modern humans spread into Europe
Had short, stocky, cold-adapted bodies and heavy brow ridges
Named for a valley in Germany where bones of one were found in 1856
Had children with early modern humans, so most people with ancestors from outside Africa carry about 1 to 2 percent of their DNA
Made stone tools, controlled fire, hunted big game, and buried their dead
Their stone tools are called Mousterian, often made with the prepared-core Levallois technique
Their brains were on average as large as or larger than ours; they had an occipital bun, a large nose, and no true chin
Their closest known relatives, the Denisovans, were identified in 2010 from a finger bone in a Siberian cave
Svante Pääbo won the 2022 Nobel Prize for ancient-DNA work, including their genome (draft published in 2010)
Quarry workers found the first recognized fossils in the Feldhofer Cave in 1856; schoolteacher Johann Carl Fuhlrott saw their importance
Their German valley honors a 17th-century preacher and hymn writer whose surname is a Greek form of “new man”
Geologist William King named them in 1864, the first extinct human group formally named from fossils
Earlier finds at Engis, Belgium (1829), and Forbes’ Quarry, Gibraltar (1848), were not recognized at first
Rudolf Virchow blamed the 1856 skeleton’s features on disease; Thomas Henry Huxley discussed it in _Evidence as to Man’s Place in Nature_ (1863)
Marcellin Boule’s stooped, apelike reconstruction of the La Chapelle-aux-Saints skeleton (found in 1908) was partly due to the man’s arthritis
In 1997, Pääbo’s team read their mitochondrial DNA from the original 1856 fossil
“Denny,” a girl known from a bone found in Denisova Cave, had a mother of their kind and a Denisovan father
They heated birch bark to make tar, a glue for attaching stone points to handles
Ralph Solecki excavated Shanidar Cave in Iraq in the 1950s: one man had survived serious injuries for years, and Solecki proposed a “flower burial”
A modern-looking hyoid bone from Kebara Cave, Israel, and the same FOXP2 gene version as ours suggest they may have been able to speak
Fossils about 430,000 years old from Spain’s Sima de los Huesos (“Pit of Bones”) belong to their early line; many think they came from _Homo heidelbergensis_
William Golding’s _The Inheritors_ (1955) and Jean M. Auel’s _The Clan of the Cave Bear_ (whose heroine is Ayla) feature them
Some of the last may have lived in Gorham’s Cave, Gibraltar, where carved crosshatch lines are thought to be theirs; at Krapina, Croatia, they may have worn eagle talons

trap.title: Which ancient humans?
trap.body: Several groups of ancient humans show up in the same tossups. Cro-Magnons were early modern humans, our own species, who reached Europe as Neanderthals were disappearing, and Denisovans were Neanderthals’ closest cousins, known mostly from DNA found in a Siberian cave. Players also guess older species like _Homo erectus_ or “Lucy,” an australopithecine who lived more than 3 million years ago.
trap.fix: A German valley, 1856, Mousterian tools, Shanidar, La Chapelle-aux-Saints, stocky cold-adapted bodies, or 1 to 2 percent of our DNA mean Neanderthals. A Siberian cave and a finger bone mean Denisovans, and cave paintings in France made by our own species point to Cro-Magnons.
trap.line: Real answer line: Neanderthals (accept Neandertals or Homo neanderthalensis; prompt on hominins or archaic humans; do not accept “Denisovans” or “Cro-Magnons”)

topics.name: Influenza virus
topics.kicker: RNA virus family behind the flu · Strains named H and N, as in H1N1
topics.briefing: The influenza virus causes the flu, a respiratory illness that comes back every winter. Its strains are named for two proteins on its surface, hemagglutinin and neuraminidase, which is why one is called H1N1. Because the virus stores its genes in eight pieces of RNA that change constantly, the vaccine has to be updated every year. A 1918 pandemic caused by one of these viruses killed tens of millions of people worldwide.
topics.answerHtml: Influenza virus (accept flu virus, Orthomyxoviridae, or influenza A; prompt on influenza, the flu, or a specific strain such as H1N1 by asking for the virus; do not accept “coronavirus” or “common cold”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Richard Shope showed in 1931 that a disease in pigs was caused by one of these agents, and two years later Wilson Smith, Christopher Andrewes, and Patrick Laidlaw isolated the first human one by infecting ferrets. Their family name combines Greek words for “straight” and “mucus.”
tossups.r: Their strains are labeled with an H number and an N number. For 10 points, name these viruses that cause a respiratory illness every winter.

tossups.p: The genome of types A and B of these viruses is split into eight separate pieces of RNA, which lets two different strains swap whole segments inside one host in a process called reassortment. That shuffling can produce a sudden big change, known as antigenic shift.
tossups.r: Smaller changes, called antigenic drift, are why their vaccine is updated yearly. For 10 points, name these viruses behind a respiratory illness that returns each winter.

tossups.p: The H in these viruses’ strain names stands for hemagglutinin [“hee-muh-GLOO-tuh-nin”], a spike that grabs sialic [“sy-AL-ik”] acid on a host cell’s surface. The N stands for neuraminidase [“noor-uh-MIN-ih-dayss”], an enzyme that snips those sugars so new copies can break free.
tossups.r: Strains are therefore labeled like H1N1. For 10 points, name these viruses that cause a respiratory illness each winter.

tossups.p: The drug oseltamivir [“oh-sel-TAM-ih-veer”] works against these agents by blocking the enzyme that lets new copies escape from a cell. Because these agents carry their genes as RNA and copy them sloppily, they change quickly and can become resistant to such drugs.
tossups.r: Their strain names use an H number and an N number. For 10 points, name these viruses behind a yearly respiratory illness.

tossups.p: Though it probably did not begin in Spain, the strain of these agents behind one pandemic became known as the “Spanish” one, because neutral Spain reported on that outbreak freely during World War I. Scientists classify that strain as an H1N1.
tossups.r: The pandemic it caused in 1918 and 1919 killed tens of millions of people worldwide. For 10 points, name these viruses that cause a respiratory illness each winter.

tossups.p: Wild aquatic birds, especially ducks and shorebirds, are the natural reservoir of type A of these agents, and pigs can catch both bird and human strains, which lets segments mix. A strain called H5N1 has spread widely in birds since the 1990s.
tossups.r: Their strains are named for two surface proteins. For 10 points, name these viruses that cause a respiratory illness in people each winter.

tossups.p: Jeffery Taubenberger’s team pieced together the genes of the 1918 strain of these agents partly from lung tissue preserved in Alaskan permafrost. They published the full sequence of that strain in 2005.
tossups.r: The 1918 pandemic strain is classified as H1N1. For 10 points, name these viruses behind a respiratory illness that returns each winter.

tossups.p: These agents come in types A, B, C, and D, but only types A and B cause major seasonal outbreaks in people, and only type A causes pandemics. Type A strains are further sorted into subtypes by their two surface proteins.
tossups.r: One such subtype is H3N2. For 10 points, name these viruses that cause a respiratory illness every winter.

tossups.p: Thomas Francis Jr. isolated type B of these agents in 1940, several years after type A was found, and he also helped make the first vaccines against them for American soldiers. Jonas Salk, who later created a polio vaccine, worked in Francis’s lab on those vaccines.
tossups.r: Their vaccine is updated every year. For 10 points, name these viruses behind a seasonal respiratory illness.

tossups.p: Twice a year, experts recommend which strains of these agents the next season’s vaccine should cover, since it takes months to grow the vaccine, often in chicken eggs. Picking the wrong strains makes the vaccine less effective, because these agents keep changing their surface proteins.
tossups.r: Those proteins give strains names like H1N1. For 10 points, name these viruses that cause a respiratory illness each winter.

tossups.p: The 1957 and 1968 pandemics caused by these agents are named for Asia and Hong Kong, and both arose when a bird strain swapped gene segments with a human strain. A 2009 pandemic strain of these agents that came from pigs was an H1N1, like the 1918 strain.
tossups.r: They store their genes in eight pieces of RNA. For 10 points, name these viruses behind a seasonal respiratory illness.

tossups.p: These agents are enveloped, meaning they wrap themselves in a piece of the host cell’s membrane studded with their own spikes. Unlike most RNA viruses, they copy their genes inside the host cell’s nucleus.
tossups.r: Their spikes are hemagglutinin and neuraminidase. For 10 points, name these viruses that cause a respiratory illness each winter.

tossups.p: The name of the illness these agents cause comes from an Italian word meaning “influence,” because people once blamed outbreaks on the stars. The illness is sometimes confused with an unrelated stomach bug and with the common cold, which is usually caused by rhinoviruses.
tossups.r: Each strain of these agents is named with an H number and an N number. For 10 points, name these viruses behind a winter respiratory illness.

tossups.p: During the 1918 pandemic, many scientists wrongly believed that a bacterium caused the illness, and one bacterium found in patients’ lungs still carries a misleading name based on that belief. Researchers in the 1930s showed instead that an agent small enough to slip through fine filters causes it.
tossups.r: Their strains have names like H1N1 and H3N2. For 10 points, name these viruses behind a seasonal respiratory illness.

tossups.p: Scientists hope to make a “universal” vaccine against these agents by targeting the stalk of their main spike protein, which changes less than its tip. Nasal spray vaccines against them use weakened versions that grow only in the cooler nose.
tossups.r: They store their genes in eight RNA segments. For 10 points, name these viruses that cause a respiratory illness each winter.

clues.t: Cause a respiratory illness that returns every winter, with fever, cough, and body aches
Strains are named for two surface proteins, giving labels like H1N1, H3N2, and H5N1
RNA viruses; like all viruses, they are not affected by antibiotics
Their vaccine must be updated every year because they keep changing
A 1918–1919 pandemic caused by one of them killed tens of millions of people worldwide
In types A and B, the genome is split into eight separate pieces of RNA
Antigenic drift: small changes each year. Antigenic shift: a sudden big change when two strains swap segments (reassortment)
The H stands for hemagglutinin, the spike that grabs sialic acid on a host cell
The N stands for neuraminidase, the enzyme that lets new copies break free from a cell
Come in types A, B, C, and D; only A and B cause major seasonal outbreaks in people, and only A causes pandemics
Wild water birds are the natural reservoir of type A, and pigs can catch both bird and human strains, letting segments mix
The drug oseltamivir blocks the enzyme that lets new copies escape a cell
The illness’s name comes from an Italian word for “influence,” because outbreaks were once blamed on the stars
Different from the common cold, which is usually caused by rhinoviruses, and from an unrelated stomach bug
Richard Shope found a pig one in 1931; Wilson Smith, Christopher Andrewes, and Patrick Laidlaw isolated the first human one in 1933 using ferrets
Their virus family’s name is built from Greek words for “straight” and “mucus”
Thomas Francis Jr. isolated type B in 1940 and, with Jonas Salk in his lab, helped develop the first vaccines against them
Jeffery Taubenberger’s team sequenced the 1918 strain, published in 2005, partly using lung tissue preserved in Alaskan permafrost
The 1918 pandemic strain, an H1N1, was called “Spanish” only because neutral Spain reported on it freely during World War I
Later pandemics: 1957 (named for Asia), 1968 (named for Hong Kong), and 2009 (an H1N1 strain that came from pigs)

trap.title: Virus, illness, or bacterium?
trap.body: Some answer lines want the virus and some want the disease, so saying just “influenza” or “the flu” may only earn a prompt when the question asks for “this virus.” The common cold is a different illness, usually caused by rhinoviruses, and a stomach bug is not the flu at all. One bacterium also carries a misleading name left over from the days when many scientists wrongly believed a bacterium caused the flu.
trap.fix: “This virus” or “these viruses” with eight RNA segments, hemagglutinin and neuraminidase spikes, or antigenic drift means the influenza virus. If a question asks for “this disease,” answer influenza, and be ready to add “virus” if you get a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Influenza virus (accept flu virus or Orthomyxoviridae; prompt on influenza, the flu, or a specific strain such as H1N1 by asking for the virus; do not accept “coronavirus” or “common cold”)
